lead: A periodic sequence has a line spectrum: a few frequencies, each with a coefficient. An aperiodic sequence has no period to pick out those lines, so its spectrum becomes a continuous curve X(e^(jω)) of frequency. That curve is the discrete-time Fourier transform (DTFT). It exists for every absolutely summable sequence, it repeats every 2π radians per sample, and one period holds all the information. Filter design, audio processing, radar and every DFT chip rest on it.
prereq: You need: the continuous-time Fourier transform and its convolution theorem (see Unit 3, Fourier Series and Fourier Transform), sampling and the spectrum of a sampled signal (see Unit 5, Sampling and Discrete-Time Systems), and the DTFS (6.1).

blocks.text: Take a sequence x[n] defined for every integer n. Its DTFT is the sum of x[n] weighted by the complex exponential e^(−jωn). The variable ω is frequency in radians per sample, not in rad/s. The two are tied by ω = ΩT, where Ω is the continuous-time frequency in rad/s and T is the sampling interval in seconds. The notation X(e^(jω)), with e^(jω) inside the bracket, is a reminder that the transform depends on ω only through the point e^(jω) on the unit circle.

blocks.where: x[n] is the sequence; ω is frequency in rad/sample; the sum runs over every integer n.

blocks.text: The inverse turns the curve back into the sequence. Integrate X(e^(jω)) e^(jωn) over any stretch of length 2π, for example ω from −π to π, and divide by 2π. The factor 1/2π belongs to the definition; drop it and the round trip no longer closes.

blocks.where: the integral runs over any interval of length 2π in ω; n is an integer.

blocks.text: Because n is an integer, e^(−j(ω+2π)n) = e^(−jωn) e^(−j2πn) = e^(−jωn). Every term of the sum repeats, so X(e^(j(ω+2π))) = X(e^(jω)). The spectrum is 2π-periodic in ω even though x[n] is not periodic at all. One period, ω in (−π, π], carries everything. The point ω = π is the Nyquist frequency, half the sampling rate.

sections.h3: Convergence and the pairs you must know

blocks.text: The sum converges uniformly, and X is a continuous function of ω, when x[n] is absolutely summable: Σ|x[n]| < ∞. Finite-length sequences qualify trivially. So does aⁿu[n] with |a| < 1, since the geometric series adds to 1/(1−|a|). Sequences with finite energy, Σ|x[n]|² < ∞, also converge, in the mean-square sense.

Some useful sequences are not absolutely summable. The unit step u[n] is the standard example. Its algebraic transform 1/(1−e^(−jω)) is finite everywhere except ω = 2πk, where it blows up. The full DTFT adds impulses of area π at those points. Writing only the fraction is a frequent error.

blocks.text: The rectangular pulse gives a Dirichlet kernel, not a sinc. For length N, X(e^(jω)) = e^(−jω(N−1)/2) sin(ωN/2)/sin(ω/2). The zeros are at ω = 2πm/N for m = 1, …, N−1 modulo N; at ω = 2πk the value is N. This kernel is the discrete cousin of the continuous rect-to-sinc pair, and it is the shape every window in spectral analysis inherits.

sections.h3: Properties, and the link to sampling

blocks.text: The convolution property is the working tool: an LTI system multiplies the spectrum point by point, so |Y| = |X||H| and the phases add. Multiplication in time becomes periodic convolution in ω, with the 1/2π factor; that is exactly how a window smears a spectrum. Parseval says the energy summed over n equals (1/2π)∫|X|²dω, so |X(e^(jω))|² is an energy density per rad/sample.
For samples x[n] = x_c(nT) of a continuous-time signal, put ω = ΩT in the DTFT. The answer is the continuous-time spectrum copied every Ω_s = 2π/T and scaled by 1/T.

blocks.where: Ω is the continuous-time frequency in rad/s, T is the sampling interval in seconds, and Ω_s = 2π/T is the sampling frequency in rad/s.

blocks.text: So the DTFT of the samples is not X_c; it is the sum of all its shifted copies. If X_c has content above Ω_s/2, the copies overlap and the overlap is aliasing (see Unit 5). The 2π repeat in ω and the Ω_s repeat in Ω are the same statement.

figure.caption: Magnitude spectra of x[n] = aⁿu[n] for a = 0.8 and a = 0.5. Both peak at ω = 0 and repeat every 2π; as a moves towards 1 the peak sharpens and low frequencies dominate.

spec.aria: Two curves peaking at ω = 0, the taller one for a = 0.8, and both curving down to a minimum at ω = ±π.

examples.question: A discrete-time signal is x[n] = (0.8)ⁿu[n]. (a) Find X(e^(jω)). (b) Write |X(e^(jω))| in closed form. (c) Evaluate the magnitude at ω = 0, ω = π/2 and ω = π rad/sample.
steps: (a) The step makes the sum start at n = 0: X(e^(jω)) = Σₙ₌₀^∞ (0.8)ⁿ e^(−jωn) = Σₙ₌₀^∞ (0.8 e^(−jω))ⁿ.
This is a geometric series with ratio r = 0.8 e^(−jω). Its modulus is |r| = 0.8 < 1, so the series converges and X(e^(jω)) = 1/(1 − 0.8 e^(−jω)).
(b) |X|² = 1/|1 − 0.8 e^(−jω)|². Expand the denominator: 1 − 1.6 cos ω + 0.64 = 1.64 − 1.6 cos ω. Hence |X| = 1/√(1.64 − 1.6 cos ω).
Sanity check: the peak sits at ω = 0 because all terms of x[n] are positive and add in phase there; the dip at ω = π comes from the alternating signs of e^(−jπn) = (−1)ⁿ.
examples.answer: X(e^(jω)) = 1/(1 − 0.8e^(−jω)); |X| = 5 at ω = 0, 0.781 at ω = π/2 and 0.556 at ω = π, with ω in rad/sample.
examples.check:
import cmath, math
a = 0.8
for w in (0.0, math.pi/2, math.pi):
    X = 1.0/(1.0 - a*cmath.exp(-1j*w))
    print(round(abs(X), 3))

traps: Writing X(jω) or X(ω). The DTFT is X(e^(jω)); the argument is a point on the unit circle and ω is in rad/sample, not rad/s.
Treating X(e^(jω)) as aperiodic and quoting one branch. The curve repeats every 2π, so the value at ω = 3π/2 equals the value at ω = −π/2.
Using 1/(1 − e^(−jω)) as the whole DTFT of u[n]. The impulses of area π at ω = 2πk are missing, and the expression is infinite there anyway.
Forgetting the 1/2π in multiplication and in Parseval. Both come straight from the inverse transform; the convolution property itself has no such factor.
Mixing up DTFT and DFT. The N-point DFT is N samples of X(e^(jω)), not X itself; a feature between the samples is invisible (6.3).

quiz.q: Write the DTFT definition and state its period in ω.
quiz.a: X(e^(jω)) = Σₙ x[n]e^(−jωn). It repeats every 2π in ω, so one period ω in (−π, π] is enough.

quiz.q: Give the DTFT of δ[n] and of δ[n−2].
quiz.a: δ[n] → 1 for all ω. δ[n−2] → e^(−j2ω), magnitude 1 and phase −2ω.

quiz.q: x[n] is aperiodic, yet X(e^(jω)) is periodic. Why?
quiz.a: Because the index n is an integer, e^(−j(ω+2π)n) = e^(−jωn)e^(−j2πn) = e^(−jωn). Every term repeats, so the sum repeats. The periodicity comes from discrete time, not from the signal.

quiz.q: Why does u[n] need impulses in its DTFT?
quiz.a: u[n] is not absolutely summable. The fraction 1/(1−e^(−jω)) is undefined at ω = 2πk, where the sequence's average value is 1/2; impulses of area π at those points supply it.

quiz.q: For x[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n], find X(e^(jω)) and |X| at ω = 0 and ω = π.
x[n] = 1 for 0 ≤ n ≤ 3 and 0 otherwise. Find X(e^(jω)) and its value at ω = 0, π/2 and π.
quiz.a: X = e^(−j3ω/2) sin(2ω)/sin(ω/2). At ω = 0 the limit is 4; at ω = π/2, sin π = 0 so X = 0; at ω = π, sin 2π = 0 so X = 0.

quiz.q: For a real even sequence x[n], show that X(e^(jω)) is real and even. Separately, use Parseval to find the energy of y[n] = (0.8)ⁿu[n].
quiz.a: Real x[n] gives X(e^(−jω)) = X*(e^(jω)); even x[n] gives X(e^(−jω)) = X(e^(jω)). Together X = X*, so X is real and even. Separately, for y[n] = (0.8)ⁿu[n], energy = Σₙ₌₀^∞(0.64)ⁿ = 1/(1−0.64) = 2.778; the frequency side gives (1/2π)∫dω/(1.64−1.6cos ω) = 1/√(1.64²−1.6²) = 1/0.36 = 2.778.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every audio equaliser, spectrum analyser and OFDM receiver evaluates X(e^(jω)) or a dense set of its samples. Software-defined radio uses the sampling relation above to fold a 2 GHz carrier down to baseband, where only the DTFT of a short record matters. The short-time Fourier transform is a DTFT of windowed frames; the periodogram is the squared magnitude of that DTFT; the cepstrum is the inverse DTFT of the log spectrum. Filter designers plot |H(e^(jω))| to read passband ripple and stopband attenuation directly off the curve. Search 'windowed DTFT', 'periodogram' and 'scipy.signal.freqz' to run these ideas on real data.
